name: Leukocyte-poor PRP

lead: Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) is made from a person's own blood, spun to concentrate platelets. Leukocyte-poor PRP is a version in which white blood cells are largely removed, a distinction researchers use to classify preparations [1].

The appearance payoff is that clinics use PRP for scalp hair thinning and skin rejuvenation, on the idea that platelet growth factors encourage healing and growth. The best-studied use is joint injection, where a 2024 randomized trial reported that leukocytes did not change safety or efficacy in knee osteoarthritis [3].

paras: In a clinic, blood is drawn, processed in a centrifuge or kit, and the resulting plasma is injected or applied, sometimes with microneedling. The number of sessions and kit type depend on the clinic.

Side effects are generally limited to injection-site pain and swelling, with infection risk when equipment is not sterile. The FDA does not regulate PRP itself, though preparation devices are cleared.

chain: Own blood is spun to concentrate platelets
Growth factors delivered to scalp or skin
Supports follicle and tissue renewal (as claimed)
angle.text: Clinics apply PRP to the scalp or face hoping to thicken hair or refresh skin. The leukocyte-poor variant is chosen by providers who prefer a purer platelet product.

lead: Leukocyte-poor PRP, also called leukocyte-reduced or pure PRP, is a platelet concentrate prepared from a person's own blood in which white blood cells are removed or minimized. A 2009 classification paper sorted platelet concentrates by leukocyte and fibrin content, listing pure PRP as a separate category from leukocyte-rich PRP and fibrin products [1].

People encounter PRP in aesthetic and hair-restoration clinics, where platelets' growth factors are used for scalp thinning and skin rejuvenation [2]. Platelet growth factors are reported to support healing [3].
Research on leukocyte content comes mainly from orthopedics. A 2024 randomized trial concluded leukocytes did not influence safety or efficacy of PRP for knee osteoarthritis [4].
infobox: Devices cleared; PRP itself not regulated

paras: PRP preparation kits differ in platelet concentration and leukocyte content, and a review found no consensus on optimal concentrations and no validated classification [3]. Leukocyte-poor products are one category in published classification systems [1].

PRP is discussed in hair-loss and facial-rejuvenation settings as a clinic-based option, often with microneedling. Within these discussions, the leukocyte-poor preparation is one of several kit types.
Trials in joints report mainly injection-site discomfort [4]. A 2024 case in which unlicensed equipment reuse was linked to infections shows sterile technique matters [2].

Most randomized trials of leukocyte-poor PRP are in knee osteoarthritis. A Japanese randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial tested leukocyte-poor PRP in mild to moderate knee osteoarthritis [5]. A 2024 double-blind randomized trial found leukocytes did not influence safety or efficacy in knee osteoarthritis [4]. The 2021 RESTORE randomized trial compared PRP with placebo for knee pain and cartilage [6]. No trial found here compared leukocyte-poor and leukocyte-rich PRP for hair or facial appearance.

timeline.event: A classification separates pure PRP (P-PRP) from leukocyte-rich platelet concentrates [1].
